name: Zane Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I drive a haul truck at the iron ore pit outside town, a 240-tonne Komatsu, twelve-hour shifts, four days on and four off. Night shift you start at six, do your pre-start checks with a torch, then it's load at the shovel, drive the ramp up to the crusher, dump, back down, maybe thirty-five loads a night. I like the quiet of it, honestly, just me and the radio and the lights of the pit. What wears me out is the fourth night, when your eyes go gritty around three in the morning and you're counting the cones on the ramp to stay awake.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside of work, what does life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Priya, she's a nurse at the district hospital, so between her rosters and mine we sometimes only see each other on the weekend. We live in my nan's old house on Railway Street, which she left me, so there's no mortgage. I've got a decent amount put away, close to a year of expenses, because the money in the pit is good and I'm not one for flash cars. I'm a union member and I go to the branch meetings at the bowls club most months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying for years: told you so. Every few months some manager stands up at the pre-shift talk with a slide about the future of mining, and nothing much changes. I'd probably post a photo of my truck with a caption like, still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but I wouldn't trust it. The company's already got driverless trucks running at the northern pit, and that's not AI hype, that's just GPS and sensors. So even if this smart chat stuff flops, the robots on the ground keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much nothing different. Keep driving, keep putting money aside, keep going to the union meetings. I'd push the branch to get a clause in the next agreement about how many crew a pit has to keep, because that fight is coming whatever the chat tools do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A bit smug, if I'm honest, but with a little knot at the back that says the trucks at the northern pit don't care if AI is hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the northern pit. Have you seen those driverless trucks yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, we did a training day up there last year. You stand at the edge of the bench and watch a truck the size of a house reverse to the shovel with nobody in it. It gives you a funny feeling in the stomach. There's a guy in an office two hundred kilometres away watching six of them on screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone on your crew want that office job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev does, he's a few years younger and he's always on his phone. Good luck to him. I'd go mad in a room with no windows, and I don't touch that AI stuff, never have, so I'm not the guy they'd pick anyway.

S0.say: I'd tell everyone I knew it was hype all along and post a photo of my truck saying I'm still here. Nothing much changes on the ramp.
S0.think: I'd be relieved but I wouldn't trust it, because the driverless trucks at the northern pit run on sensors and GPS, not hype. The robots keep coming either way.
S0.do: Keeps driving and keeps putting money aside. Pushes his union branch to fight for a minimum crew clause in the next agreement, because he thinks that fight is coming anyway.
S0.feel: Settled and a little smug, with a small knot of worry about the driverless trucks.
S0.quote: You stand at the edge of the bench and watch a truck the size of a house reverse to the shovel with nobody in it.
S0.fieldNote: Zane separates 'AI' from 'robots' very clearly; for him the real threat is already visible at the northern pit and has nothing to do with chat tools. He has no mortgage and close to a year saved, so even this mild picture gets read through a union lens. He rules himself out of the remote control room before anyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, right, this is when the union earns its fees. I'd be the one at the branch meeting saying we need a deal on retraining and redundancy before they roll out the next lot of driverless trucks, not after. Online I'd probably share stuff about the shareholders getting richer while crews get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my truck seat is one of the first to go. Driving a haul truck in a pit is the easiest thing in mining to automate, it's the same loop all night. I'd probably last a few years because they convert the fleet one pit at a time, but I wouldn't be driving at thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving as long as they'll have me, and I'd put more in savings, maybe up from a quarter of my pay to a third. I'd go for the delegate role at the union so I'm in the room when they talk about it. I'm not going to rush off and do some course in drones or whatever; I'd rather stay and fight for a fair deal for everyone on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being told there's weather coming. You can't stop it but you can tie stuff down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Everyone on the crew is in the same spot. Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Kev, who's fifty-eight and has driven trucks since before I was born. He's got a mortgage on a block out past the racecourse and he can barely send a text. If they convert our pit he's done, and nobody's going to retrain Kev into a control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do a course. If the union got the company to pay for retraining, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it to be there for people. For me, I don't know. I've got a year of savings and a house with no loan on it, so I'm the guy who can afford to be stubborn, and maybe that's the problem. I'd probably wait until they forced it.

S1.say: I'd say this is when the union earns its fees and push for a retraining and redundancy deal before the next lot of driverless trucks arrives. Online I'd share posts about shareholders getting richer while crews shrink.
S1.think: He thinks a haul truck seat is one of the easiest jobs in mining to automate and expects to be out of the cab within a few years. He only expects to hang on because pits get converted one at a time.
S1.do: Raises his savings from a quarter to about a third of his pay and stands for union delegate to be in the room. Keeps driving and puts off any retraining until the company forces it.
S1.feel: Like a storm warning: he can't stop it, so he braces and gets ready.
S1.quote: I've got a year of savings and a house with no loan on it, so I'm the guy who can afford to be stubborn, and maybe that's the problem.
S1.fieldNote: He admits, with some self-awareness, that his savings and paid-off house are what let him be stubborn. His worry turns quickly to older crew like Kev rather than himself. Retraining is something he wants available for others but keeps pushing away for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. At work I'd say they need to stop the rollout until there's a plan, and I'd be at any protest at the company office in the city. Online I'd be the guy posting that a few billionaires own the robots now and the rest of us should be asking for a share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in mining inside a year or so of it landing. If a robot can do anything a person can, then the shovel, the dozer, the fitters, the lot goes. I'm twenty-seven, so it's not like I can ride it out till a pension; I'd have forty years left with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Priya and work out how long my savings plus her wage covers us, and I'd stop spending on anything extra, no new pickup, no trip to the coast we'd planned. I'd go all in with the union and whatever political party is talking about taxing the robot owners. I don't know what job I'd even train for, if a robot does it all, so I'm not wasting money on a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't much warning. What would you do in those two years, before it fully lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the thing, two years is nothing. Our enterprise agreement runs three years, so it'd land in the middle of it and we'd have nothing to bargain with. I'd be trying to get a whole union to move faster than a company that already owns the robots. We'd lose that race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the money in the bank changes for you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me time, that's all. Priya's job might be safer than mine, people still want a human nurse I think, so we wouldn't starve. But I'd feel like a kept man and I'd hate that.

S2.say: He'd call for the rollout to stop until there's a plan and join protests outside the company's city office. Online he'd say a few billionaires own the robots and everyone else should get a share.
S2.think: He believes he'd be out of mining within a year of it landing, along with everyone else at the pit. At twenty-seven he can't ride it out to a pension and sees forty years with nothing to do.
S2.do: Works out with Priya how long his savings and her wage would last, and cancels the new pickup and the coast trip. Throws himself into union action and backs any party pushing to tax robot owners, but won't pay for a course.
S2.feel: Sick, like the floor has gone out from under him.
S2.quote: I'd be trying to get a whole union to move faster than a company that already owns the robots. We'd lose that race.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year timing hits him through a union calendar: the agreement runs three years, so he feels there'd be nothing left to bargain with. Money makes him safe from hunger but not from shame; he dreads being a 'kept man'. He refuses to retrain because he can't see a target job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as the fast one, but I'd be saying it for longer. I'd be on at the union to use the next agreement round to lock in job guarantees and a payout tied to how much the robots save them. Online I'd be sharing every story about a pit going driverless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a bit more breathing room, but it ends the same place. I'd be thirty-two with nothing that a robot can't do. The difference is I'd see it coming, which is almost worse, watching it creep across the pit one truck at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and save hard, aim for two years of expenses by the time it lands. I'd use the next agreement in 2028 to fight for a big redundancy formula, so at least when it goes we walk out with something. I might look at buying a second small house on Railway Street to rent out, so there's some money that isn't a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but less sick than the two-year one. More like dread than shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives us one proper bargaining round instead of none. Five years means I get to watch my own job get packed up, truck by truck. Two years would just be a punch. Five is a slow squeeze, but at least we can make them pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about a rental house. Isn't that a bit like being an owner yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, yeah, Priya said the same. It's not like owning a robot fleet, it's one old weatherboard house. But fair point, I'd be looking out for myself as well as the crew, I won't pretend I wouldn't.

S3.say: He'd push the union to use the next agreement round to lock in job guarantees and a payout tied to what the robots save the company. Online he'd keep sharing stories of pits going driverless.
S3.think: He thinks five years gives a bit more room but ends in the same place, with him at thirty-two and nothing a robot can't do. Seeing it creep across the pit truck by truck feels almost worse.
S3.do: Keeps driving and saves towards two years of expenses. Fights in the 2028 agreement for a strong redundancy formula, and looks at buying a second small house on Railway Street to rent out.
S3.feel: Dread rather than shock: heavy, but less sick than the two-year picture.
S3.quote: Five years means I get to watch my own job get packed up, truck by truck. Two years would just be a punch.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years matter to him mainly because they give the union one real bargaining round. He is candid when challenged about the rental house being a small form of ownership. His plan is to extract a good exit, not to change careers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd be telling people we've got no excuse, we can organise properly this time. I'd say it at the branch, I'd say it at the pub. I'd want laws in place well before 2036 about what happens to towns like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is different, I'll admit that. I'd be thirty-seven, and that's young enough to do something else, I just don't know what. Part of me thinks I'd ride the truck for another eight years, take the money, and deal with it then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep saving, and I'd buy that rental house in the first couple of years while prices are steady. I'd run for the branch committee and push for a fund paid for by the robot owners that keeps the town going. Maybe around year five I'd look at something with people, like Priya keeps saying, aged care or the ambulance service, but I'd want to see what's actually left first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steadier. Ten years feels like enough to fight in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said around year five you might look at aged care or ambulance. What would make you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first fully robot pit in our region running without a single person on site. That'd be my sign. Priya says I'd be a good paramedic because I don't panic at three in the morning, and I don't, I just hate change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And who would you blame, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the robots, they're just machines. The people who decide the profits go to shareholders in another country and the town gets a plaque. That's a choice, and governments could make a different one.

S4.say: With ten years he'd tell people at the branch and the pub that there's no excuse not to organise properly. He'd want laws in place well before 2036 about what happens to mining towns.
S4.think: He admits ten years is different: he'd be thirty-seven, young enough to do something else. Part of him would ride the truck for eight more years, take the money and deal with it then.
S4.do: Keeps driving, buys the rental house in the first couple of years and runs for the union branch committee to push for a town fund paid by robot owners. Around year five, if a fully robot pit opens nearby, considers training for aged care or the ambulance service.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steadier; ten years feels like enough time to fight.
S4.quote: Priya says I'd be a good paramedic because I don't panic at three in the morning, and I don't, I just hate change.
S4.fieldNote: Time softens him more than anything else in the interview: with a decade he can picture a second career, as long as there's a clear signal first. He blames choices made by owners and governments, not the machines. Priya is the one nudging him towards caring work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easy. There's no time for the union to do anything and no time for a town to plan. What would help is a law that says if you replace a crew with robots, part of what you save goes back to that crew and that town for years, not a one-off payout. I don't need a handout, I've got savings. I need the company to not get to just walk away from the town.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. Half the shops on the main street are there because of pit wages. If the trucks drive themselves, the bakery goes too, and nobody's counting that.

headlineQuote: I don't need a handout, I've got savings. I need the company to not get to just walk away from the town.
portrait: Zane is a 27-year-old haul truck driver at an open-pit iron ore mine who lives with his partner Priya, a nurse, in his late grandmother's mortgage-free house. He likes the quiet of night shift, avoids AI tools entirely and already sees driverless trucks at a nearby pit as the real threat. Through every scenario he leans on the union and politics rather than retraining, and he knows his savings are what let him be stubborn. The fast AGI picture alarms him because there'd be no bargaining round; with ten years he can just about picture becoming a paramedic.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time for the union to bargain or for the town to plan.
whatWouldHelp: A law that sends part of what a company saves by replacing a crew back to that crew and town for years, not a one-off payout.
